title: Gabber splitting of relative central extensions of SL2
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] and $Z$ a separated commutative $S$-group scheme: a group object over $S$ with commutative multiplication and closed diagonal [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Let $E$ be a sheaf of groups for the fppf topology on $S$-schemes, whose coverings are faithfully flat finitely presented jointly surjective families. Suppose there is a central exact sequence of fppf sheaves $$1\longrightarrow Z\xrightarrow{i}E\xrightarrow{p}\operatorname{SL}_{2,S}\longrightarrow1.$$ Exact means that $i$ identifies $Z$ with the kernel of $p$ and sections of the target lift fppf-locally; central means that $i(Z)$ commutes with all sections of $E$ after every base change. For an $S$-scheme $U$, $\operatorname{SL}_{2,S}(U)$ is the determinant-one $2\times2$ matrices in $\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$. There exists a unique homomorphism of sheaves $s:\operatorname{SL}_{2,S}\to E$ with $p\circ s=\mathrm{id}$. The map $(z,g)\mapsto i(z)s(g)$ is an isomorphism $Z\times_S\operatorname{SL}_{2,S}\simeq E$. In particular $E$ is represented by an $S$-scheme, and when $E$ is already represented the splitting is a morphism of $S$-group schemes. No smoothness of $Z$ or $E$ and no assumption that $2$ is invertible is required.

source.place: Conrad, Proposition 4.3.1 (Gabber) and proof, printed pp.126--131. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this relative structural theorem.

proof.text: Put $G=\operatorname{SL}_{2,S}$, with $x(u),y(v),h(t)$ as in the cited root-relation lemma, and $D=h(\mathbf G_m)$. Let $D',U',V'$ be the inverse images in $E$ of $D,x(\mathbf G_a),y(\mathbf G_a)$. For $a,b\in D$ choose fppf-local lifts $A,B\in D'$ and define $c(a,b)=[A,B]$. The commutator lies in $Z$; replacing either lift by a central element does not change it, so these local sections glue. Because all these commutators are central, $[AA',B]=[A,B][A',B]$ and $[A,BB']=[A,B][A,B']$. Thus $c:D\times D\to Z$ is multiplicative in each variable. This natural transformation is a scheme morphism since both its source and target are represented. Apply the torus-pairing vanishing lemma through $h:\mathbf G_m\simeq D$. Hence every such commutator is one and $D'$ is commutative.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, p.127, preimages of D,U,V and commutativity of D-prime.

proof.text: Conjugation by a local lift of $g\in G$ is independent of its lift, because any two differ by a central element of $Z$; local lifts therefore give an action of $G$ on $E$. Its restriction to $D$ preserves $U'$ and $V'$ and fixes $Z$. Direct multiplication of determinant-one matrices gives $h(t)x(u)h(t)^{-1}=x(t^2u)$ and $h(t)y(v)h(t)^{-1}=y(t^{-2}v)$. The weighted-additive lemma applies to $U'\to\mathbf G_a$ with $k=2$ and to $V'\to\mathbf G_a$ with $k=-2$. Obtain equivariant homomorphisms $x',y':\mathbf G_a\to E$ lifting $x,y$. No representability of $U',V'$ is assumed here.

Define $g'(t)=y'(-t^{-1})x'(t)y'(-t^{-1})$ and $h'(t)=g'(t)g'(1)^{-1}$. Step 1 verifies the commutative-preimage hypothesis of the lifted-root lemma; Step 2 verifies both equivariant homomorphism hypotheses. It follows that $h'$ is a homomorphism lifting $h$, and that the two Gauss relations of that lemma hold whenever $1+uv$ is invertible. In particular its inverse-form relation is available even when either additive parameter is zero or a nonunit.

On the open cell $\Omega$ of the extension lemma define $\sigma(x(u)h(s)y(v))=x'(u)h'(s)y'(v)$. The coordinates are unique: if the matrix entries are $a,b,c,d$ and $d$ is invertible, they are $s=d^{-1},u=b/d,v=c/d$. Thus this formula is a natural map, lifts the inclusion of $\Omega$ into $G$, and sends $1$ to $1$. To check partial multiplicativity, take two coordinate triples $(u,s,v)$ and $(a,t,b)$, and put $w=1+va$. Their matrix product lies in $\Omega$ exactly when $w$ is a unit, since its bottom-right entry is $s^{-1}wt^{-1}$. The inverse-form Gauss relation rewrites its lifted middle factors as $y'(v)x'(a)=x'(a/w)h'(w)^{-1}y'(v/w)$. Conjugating by the diagonal lifts and combining adjacent additive and multiplicative factors gives
$$\sigma(x(u)h(s)y(v))\sigma(x(a)h(t)y(b))=x'(u+s^2a/w)h'(st/w)y'(b+t^2v/w).$$
The identical matrix multiplication yields the coordinates $(u+s^2a/w,st/w,b+t^2v/w)$ downstairs. This proves the required equality whenever the product remains in $\Omega$.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, p.130: partial multiplication on the open cell; reordering written explicitly.

proof.text: Apply the open-cell extension lemma with $H=E$ and the map $\sigma$ just constructed. It gives a homomorphism $s:G\to E$. The two homomorphisms $p\circ s$ and $\mathrm{id}_G$ have the same restriction to $\Omega$, so uniqueness in the same lemma, now with $H=G$, gives $p\circ s=\mathrm{id}_G$.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, pp.130--131: extension to a splitting.

proof.text: If $s_1,s_2:G\to E$ are splittings, their ratio $s_2(g)s_1(g)^{-1}$ lies in $Z$. Centrality shows by multiplying two such expressions that this ratio defines a homomorphism $f:G\to Z$. Commutativity of $Z$ makes $f$ invariant under conjugation by $D$. Consequently $f\circ x$ is invariant for weight $2$, and $f\circ y$ for weight $-2$; the final assertion of the weighted-additive lemma makes both trivial. Matrix multiplication gives $g(t)=y(-t^{-1})x(t)y(-t^{-1})$ and $h(t)=g(t)g(1)^{-1}$, so $f\circ h=1$ also. Thus $f=1$ on $\Omega$, and uniqueness in the open-cell extension lemma with $H=Z$ makes $f=1$ on all of $G$. Hence $s_1=s_2$.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, pp.126--127, uniqueness, using equivariant additive vanishing instead of schematic-density reduction.

proof.text: The natural map $Z\times_SG\to E$, $(z,g)\mapsto i(z)s(g)$, is a homomorphism by centrality. Its inverse sends $e$ to $(z,p(e))$, where $i(z)=e\,s(p(e))^{-1}$; the kernel identification supplies a unique such section $z$, compatibly with restriction. Substitution checks both composites are identities. The product $Z\times_SG$ is an $S$-scheme, so this is a representation of $E$. If $E$ was already represented, a natural map $G\to E$ is a morphism of $S$-schemes: evaluate the transformation at the identity point of $G$ to obtain that morphism, and naturality identifies its value on every $T$-point. Its homomorphism identities make it a morphism of group schemes. The arguments used neither smoothness of $Z,E$ nor inversion of $2$.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, p.126, representability consequence; explicit inverse and functor-of-points verification.

lean.statement: theorem relativeSL2_central_extension_splitting {S : Scheme.{u}} (Z : Grp (Over S)) [IsCommMonObj Z.X] [IsClosedImmersion (pullback.diagonal Z.X.hom)] (E : Sheaf (Scheme.fppfTopology.over S) GrpCat.{max u v}) (i : (yonedaGrp.obj Z ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) ⟶ E.obj) (p : E.obj ⟶ relativeSL2Presheaf S ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) (hi : ∀ U : (Over S)ᵒᵖ, Function.Injective (i.app U)) (hker : ∀ (U : (Over S)ᵒᵖ) (e : E.obj.obj U), p.app U e = 1 ↔ ∃ z, i.app U z = e) (hp : Presheaf.IsLocallySurjective (Scheme.fppfTopology.over S) p) (hcentral : ∀ (U : (Over S)ᵒᵖ) (z : (yonedaGrp.obj Z ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}).obj U) (e : E.obj.obj U), i.app U z * e = e * i.app U z) : ∃ s : (relativeSL2Presheaf S ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) ⟶ E.obj, s ≫ p = 𝟙 _ ∧ (∀ s' : (relativeSL2Presheaf S ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) ⟶ E.obj, s' ≫ p = 𝟙 _ → s' = s) ∧ (∀ U : (Over S)ᵒᵖ, ∃ e : ((yonedaGrp.obj Z ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}).obj U × (relativeSL2Presheaf S ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}).obj U) ≃* E.obj.obj U, ∀ z g, e (z, g) = i.app U z * s.app U g) ∧ (E.obj ⋙ forget GrpCat).IsRepresentable ∧ (∀ (G H : Grp (Over S)) (α : (yonedaGrp.obj G ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) ≅ relativeSL2Presheaf S ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) (β : (yonedaGrp.obj H ⋙ GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u}) ≅ E.obj), ∃ t : G ⟶ H, Functor.whiskerRight (yonedaGrp.map t) GrpCat.uliftFunctor.{v, u} ≫ β.hom = α.hom ≫ s)
